title: Adaptive Exponent Tracking and Stitching for Stable Mixed-Precision Accumulation
content:
Summary:

This note proposes a practical, low-overhead approach for preventing NaNs and large-variance numeric drift in mixed-precision inference by tracking per-layer and per-activation exponent statistics ("exponent tracking"), and applying lightweight scaling "stitching" across layer boundaries and KV-cache reuse boundaries. The goal is a safe, incrementally deployable set of kernel and scheduler changes that reduce the incidence of inf/NaN and maintain stable logits without resorting to always-upgrade-to-fp32 accumulation (too costly).

Motivation / Observed Failures:
- In long-context chat workloads we still see rare NaNs and divergence after repeated prefix reuse from KV cache; root cause often small, repeated scaling mismatches that accumulate in attention/FFN accumulators.
- Mixed-precision (int8/fp16/fp8) reductions plus fused matmul kernels occasionally overflow a shared accumulator when an unusual token triggers a large activation.
- Prefetching and scheduling that runs prefix kv lines on different accelerators than the current decode step can cause exponent context discontinuities (different per-device kernel scaling heuristics).
- Current mitigations (global clamp, fallback to fp32 for whole layer) are heavy-handed and hurt throughput. We need finer-grained, robust mechanics.

Design overview (high level):
1) Per-layer exponent tracker state: small 16-bit state stored with model metadata and per-worker cache that records a running histogram of observed exponents (or highest exponent seen) for key tensors: attention scores, attention outputs, FFN pre-linear, and outputs. This is updated cheaply per batch with saturating counters.

2) Stitching operations at layer boundaries and KV-cache reuse points: when a request reuses prefix kv from an earlier run, compare exponent summaries between current run and cached prefix. If mismatch exceeds threshold, insert a micro-scale rescale kernel that applies a single scalar multiplier (power-of-two preferred) to align exponents before accumulation. This avoids re-evaluating prefix or switching to fp32.

3) Accumulator saturation monitor + soft fallback: kernels expose a lightweight probe that reports if an accumulator saturation event was observed. If observed, the runtime can do one of: a) re-run only the offending matmul in higher-precision, b) apply stitched rescale upstream and replay the dependent ops, or c) progressively broaden the scope to full layer fp32 if needed. Preference: smallest replay possible.

4) Kernel fusion changes: provide fused path that does matmul + scaling + write-back to KV with atomic exponent update. The atomic operation stores the post-scale exponent summary into the per-layer tracker so future runs see the aligned value.

5) Scheduler hints: prefer colocating decode and prefix-serving kernels when the prefix exponent variance is high. Add an affinity hint computed from exponent-tracker variance to the scheduler so that high variance contexts avoid cross-device prefix reuse.

KV-cache interactions (details):
- Store exponent summary alongside key/value tensors in the cache. When reading KV entries, the load path returns (kv_tensor, kv_exponent). The current decode step compares kv_exponent to local_exponent and decides whether to stitch.
- Because most prefixes are stable, checks should be cheap: compare 8-bit exponents or a small fingerprint. Fallback frequency is expected <0.1% in normal workloads if thresholds tuned.

Microbenchmarks & Success Criteria:
- Objective: reduce inf/NaN incidents by >95% across our sampled workloads while keeping average per-token latency overhead <1% and p99 <5% relative to baseline fused int8 path.
- Benchmarks to run: long chat sessions (8k tokens) with adversarial prompts, beam-search style decoding with many candidate tokens, and stress tests that inject extreme token activations.
- Metrics: NaN/Inf counts, soft-clamp events, extra replays per token, latency delta (avg/p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec), and token-level KL to fp32 baseline to measure numeric fidelity.

Implementation plan (staged):
Phase 0 (instrumentation): add accumulator-saturation probe and per-layer exponent metrics to kernels; do no automatic rescale. Roll this out widely to collect baseline stats. (2–3 weeks)

Phase 1 (stitch + offline replay): implement stitching kernels and KV exponents but keep them opt-in via config. On mismatch, record and optionally run a debug replay to measure correctness impact, but do not automatically rescale. (3–4 weeks)

Phase 2 (auto-stitch with small scope replay): enable automatic per-matmul stitching and single-op replays in runtime for detected saturation events; add scheduler affinity hint. Monitor. (3–4 weeks)

Phase 3 (graceful broad fallback): add progressive fallback logic (single-op -> layer -> fp32) and safety gates (circuit breaker when too many replays occur). (2 weeks)

Kernel-level notes and proposals:
- Represent exponent summaries as unsigned 8-bit biased exponents (min overhead). Update with atomic max on write-back.
- Rescale multipliers should be power-of-two where possible to avoid extra FP rounding noise; allow small non-power-of-two scaling for rare adjusments when necessary (configurable).
- Provide a "cheap replay" API that re-runs one matmul on demand with higher accumulation precision without tearing down the rest of the execution. Requires idempotent matmul kernels and preserved inputs in device-local scratch.

Scheduler interactions and heuristics:
- Exponent-variance score (EVS): a small scalar computed from per-layer tracker (e.g., top-quantile exponent delta) used as scheduling weight. If EVS > threshold, we prefer same-device placement and avoid cross-device prefix stitching.
- For multi-tenant hosts, EVS cost is accounted as expected replay overhead. Scheduler should prefer to place high-EVS requests on capacity with spare headroom.

Open questions / risks:
- How much storage overhead for exponent summaries in KV cache is acceptable? (8-bit per cached KV element may be fine, but multiply by model size for very long contexts)
- Edge cases where rescale causes small bias in softmax logits over many steps — need to monitor KL and downstream generation quality.
- Interaction with quantized models (e.g., per-channel int8): stitching across channels may be more complex than a single scalar; may need per-channel sketches for some layers.
- Security: ensure no attacker can craft tokens that force repeated replays and DoS the system (rate-limiting and circuit breakers required).

Telemetry and rollout gating:
- Gate on reduction of NaN events in canary with heavy-tail users disabled for first 48 hours. Thresholds: if auto-replay rates >0.1% tokens or average replay latency >3ms, rollback.
- Telemetry: counters for probe hits, stitch events, replays (by scope), and latencies. Store histograms and sample traces for problematic sessions.

Next steps / TODOs:
- PR: runtime API for cheap-replay (ENG-1245) (Marco)
- Kernel: implement exponent atomic update and probe (Priya)
- Scheduler: accept EVS hints (Ethan)
- Bench: assemble adversarial prompt corpus and run long-context stress tests (Samantha)

Notes to self:
- Keep the initial rollout conservative; prefer observability first.
- We should pair with model-onboarding team to tag models with known high-dynamic-range activations.

References / past experiments: this builds on prior rescale/reduce proposals but focuses on incremental, local stitching and scheduler-aware placement. See linked GH PR for early prototype and Slack thread for recent failure traces.

End of doc.
